To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
astrocyte cultures maintained in serum-free medium support CMV and HIV-1 gene expression and viral replication.
serum-containing medium supports fibroblast proliferation in human fetal astro-cyte cultures, which may confound neurovirological assays of viral gene expression.
astrocyte cultures prepared from human fetal brain tissue and maintained in a serum-free medium supplemented with FGF-2 support productive viral replication and gene expression assays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of astrocyte cultures which support productive viral replication and gene expression assays, while minimizing contamination with fibroblast cell types.
the development of astrocyte culture systems for the study of neurotropic viruses.
the use of highly enriched astrocytes to study the molecular biology of viral gene expression in the human CNS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the media used for astrocyte culturing can influence the viral gene expression assay results in astrocyte cultures.

the astrocytic cultures in B16/FGF-2 medium provide a more homogeneous population of astrocytes that are less likely to be contaminated by fibroblasts, and that this may be an important consideration when interpreting results of in vitro neurovirologic studies.

the use of serum-free media in neurovirological assays can be expected to yield more reliable results than serum-containing media, and the use of astrocyte-enriched cultures in neurovirology assays is recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
astrocyte cultures maintained in serum-free B16/FGF-2 medium are highly enriched in astrocytes and support viral gene expression assays that accurately reflect astrocyte viral gene expression.
the astrocyte cultures developed and maintained in B16/FGF-2 medium support viral replication and transient gene expression studies, while cultures maintained in serum containing medium do not.
serum-containing medium is not suitable for astrocyte culture for neurovirology studies, and serum-free defined medium supplemented with FGF-2 is the preferred medium for such studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
serum-free defined medium supports highly enriched astrocytes that are useful for in vitro neurovirology studies.
serum-free medium is critical to the maintenance of astrocyte purity in CNS cultures and to the performance of viral gene expression assays.
the medium in which human CNS-derived astrocyte cultures are maintained can influence viral gene expression.
